title: Fungi
status: draft: written 18 Nov 2026 offline for Grade 6 Science and Technology; not yet checked by a CBC Science and Technology teacher; not loaded by the live tutor
notes: Grow moulds first: a slice of damp bread and an orange peel in a closed clear bag for a week (never opened, thrown away sealed). Bring market mushrooms, a packet of baker's yeast and a sachet of yeast with sugar in warm water so the child sees the froth.

skills.key_step: The child names a fungus from its description or picture (mushroom, toadstool, puffball, yeast, mould) and counts yeast and moulds as fungi.

floor.prerequisite: Knows plants are living things that make their own food.
floor.question: Where does a plant make its food?

representations: market mushrooms and a sealed bag of mouldy bread
yeast froth in warm sugary water
a picture chart of five fungi
steps: Look at each: mushroom, toadstool, puffball, yeast, mould.
Note what they share: no green colour, grow on food or dead matter.
Yeast froths; mould is fuzzy on food.
contexts: mushrooms in a forest after rain

board.do: Draw a mushroom, a fuzzy patch on bread and a cup of froth.

board.say: Is this dirt or a living thing?

board.do: Wait for the child to decide.

misconceptions.ask: Is a mushroom green? Does it have leaves?
misconceptions.repair: Fungi are not plants: no green colour, no leaves.

misconceptions.ask: Did the fuzzy patch grow bigger each day?
misconceptions.repair: Mould is a living fungus that grows.

misconceptions.ask: Why does yeast froth in warm sugary water?
misconceptions.repair: Yeast is a living fungus that feeds and makes gas.

misconceptions.ask: What do mould, yeast and mushrooms share?
misconceptions.repair: Fungi include yeast, moulds and puffballs.

checks.question: Name two fungi other than mushrooms.
checks.answer: any two: yeast, bread mould, puffball, toadstool

skills.key_step: The child says how fungi differ from green plants: no chlorophyll, so they cannot make food; they feed on dead or living matter; no roots, stems or leaves; they reproduce by spores.

floor.question: Name one fungus.
floor.answer: for example a mushroom or yeast

steps: Food: plants make it, fungi take it from what they grow on.
Body: no roots, stems or leaves; threads instead.

board.do: Draw a table: plant and fungus, rows colour, food, parts, new ones from.
Point at the fungus food row.
board.say: Where does a mushroom get its food?

board.do: Wait for "from the log it grows on".
Ask the child to fill in the rest.

misconceptions.ask: Is a mushroom green? Can it make food without green?
misconceptions.repair: Fungi cannot make food; they feed on other things.

misconceptions.ask: Does the mushroom have leaves to make food?
misconceptions.repair: Fungi have no true roots, stems or leaves.

misconceptions.ask: Why are some mushrooms called poisonous?
misconceptions.repair: Some fungi are poisonous; never eat wild mushrooms.

misconceptions.ask: Does the dust have a store of food like a bean?

checks.question: Why can a mushroom grow in a dark place where plants cannot?
checks.answer: it does not make its own food, so it does not need light

skills.key_step: The child describes how fungi are useful (food, baking and brewing with yeast, medicine such as penicillin, rotting dead matter into soil) and harmful (food spoilage, plant and human diseases).

floor.prerequisite: Knows fungi feed on other things.
floor.question: What do fungi feed on?

steps: Yeast makes gas that raises dough.
Fungi rot dead things into soil.
Some cause disease (ringworm, crop rusts) and spoil food.

board.do: Draw dough before and after an hour with yeast.
Ask what made the dough bigger.
Draw bubbles in the dough and write "gas from yeast".

misconceptions.ask: What are the holes in bread?
misconceptions.repair: Yeast makes a gas that raises dough.

misconceptions.ask: Which fungus do we eat? Which helps bread?
What would happen to fallen leaves with no fungi?
misconceptions.repair: Fungi rot dead things into soil.

checks.question: Give two uses of fungi.
checks.answer: any two: food, baking, medicine, rotting dead matter

checks.question: Give one harmful effect of fungi.
checks.answer: spoil food, cause diseases in people or crops

skills.key_step: The child says mould grows from spores in the air on damp, warm food, and prevents it by keeping food dry, cool, covered and eating it in time.

floor.question: Is the fuzz on old bread living?

representations: sealed bags: damp bread, dry bread, bread in a cool place
a results table over a week
a picture of spores in the air
steps: Spores are always in the air.
They grow on food that is damp and warm.
Dry, cool, covered food grows less mould.
Throw mouldy food away; scraping is not safe.
contexts: a lunch box left in the sun

board.do: Draw three sealed bags: damp bread, dry bread, bread in a cool place.
Ask which will grow the most mould.
Shade the damp bread bag the most.

listen_for: dry food in the sun goes mouldy
misconceptions.ask: Which bag grew the most mould?
misconceptions.repair: Mould grows best on damp, warm food.

listen_for: scrape it off and eat it
misconceptions.ask: Can the mould threads go deep into the bread?
misconceptions.repair: Mould spreads inside; throw the food away.

misconceptions.ask: Where did the spores come from?
misconceptions.repair: Spores come from the air and land on food.

misconceptions.ask: Did the fridge bread go mouldy in the end?
misconceptions.repair: Cold slows mould; it does not kill it.

checks.question: Give two conditions that help mould grow on food.
Give one way to stop mould growing on stored maize.
checks.answer: dry it well before storing, or keep it dry and cool
